Your grandsire Aldous married Maud Fenn, a miller's daughter, in your own chapel, and Brother Osric will swear to it before Dame Crowe. Resolves to confess the false descent to Dame Crowe and rest on the plain land-grant, with Osric's testimony.
Day 2, ~6:30 PM: dismissed by Lord Edric and sent to his chamber under watch of the gate guard. Garrow slipped out in the confusion. Hale's last look at Wren was not a smile.

entries.text:
Lord Edric takes the sheet with shaking hands and reads it twice, his lips moving. Your Persuasion check was a 13, and it's enough. "Aldous... and a miller's daughter," he whispers. Then, unexpectedly, he laughs, a cracked, wet sound. "My grandmother used to say the best bread in Thornhallow was her mother's. I thought it was a joke." He lifts his eyes to Hale, and the weariness in them hardens into something new.

"Hale. Why did you want that book?"

"My lord, I only..."

"And Garrow. I never hired a carpenter."

Hale's smile holds for a breath, then another. When Lord Edric calls the gate-guard from the stair, it finally lets go. Hale says nothing at all. He bows, precisely, and is walked away to his chamber with a guard at his door. At the corner of the passage he looks back at you. It isn't a smile.

The kitchen door bangs somewhere below. Garrow has slipped out in the confusion, and you doubt he's gone far.

Lord Edric sinks into his chair and holds the register copy to his chest. "I will tell Dame Crowe myself. The land is mine by deed, and I will not hide behind a lie any longer. Brother Osric will stand beside me?" He looks up at you, tired and, for the first time, a little lighter. "You came back to us, child. What do you want for it?"

It's evening on the second day, and Dame Crowe arrives at noon the day after tomorrow. Corvin is still somewhere upriver, and your stolen ledger is still hidden in the psalter's binding. What does Wren say?

Wren's Persuasion (8) on Hale failed to make him act: he won't dismiss Hale tonight, afraid to lose his only clerk before the assessor; he orders Hale confined to his quarters and Garrow out of the manor, but is shaken and tells Wren to bring Osric's sworn attestation by morning.

entries.text:
You press the copy into Lord Edric's hands and plant yourself between him and Hale. He reads it with his lips moving, once, then again. When he reaches the bride's plain name, his shoulders drop, and what crosses his face is mostly relief. "A miller's daughter," he whispers. "Maud Fenn. My grandmother. I remember her bread." He laughs once, unsteadily, and wipes his eyes. "The land is ours by deed. It was never the line."

Then you turn him toward Hale, and your Persuasion check, an 8, stumbles. Hale doesn't hurry. "My lord," he says, gentle as a physician, "you've had a long, frightening week, and a stranger is putting words in your mouth. The hedge-carpenter was hired by me to guard the road, as you permitted. The book was only my concern for your safety." He bows. "Of course, if you no longer trust me..."

Lord Edric looks at him a long moment, and you can see that he wants to dismiss him and is afraid to. Hale has run his accounts for years. "Not tonight," he says at last, and his voice shakes. "Hale, you will keep to your rooms until the assessor has come and gone. Garrow leaves the manor at once." Hale bows again, smiling, and goes without a word. His eyes touch yours on the way past, pleasant and entirely cold.

Lord Edric turns back to you, hands trembling around the paper. "Bring me Brother Osric's sworn word by morning, child, and we'll decide what to tell Dame Crowe. I'll have a bed made ready for you." Tobin sags against the wall, openly weeping with relief.

It is nearly seven in the evening. Hale is confined, not beaten. Garrow will be on the road, possibly toward Corvin. The assessor is a day and a half away.

You step inside, press the copy into Lord Edric's hands, and plant yourself between him and Hale. Your Persuasion check was a natural 1, and it goes badly.

Lord Edric reads, and his lips move over Maud Fenn's name. Something in him eases. "A miller's daughter," he whispers. "Grandfather's Maud. I remember her bread." But when you press on Hale, his eyes flick to the steward, and old habit takes over. Hale doesn't deny a thing. He is gentle and reasonable, a sorrowing servant.

"Garrow guards the roads for the household's sake, my lord. And the book? I only wished to keep a forger's ledger from doing you harm. Would a man who meant ill have waited for your lordship's apprentice to arrive?" He sighs. "The girl is clever. She has Corvin's tongue. I fear she has used it on you."

Edric's hands shake. He is a man who has leaned on this voice for years, and he can't bring himself to throw it off with a stranger watching. "Enough," he says hoarsely. "Both of you. The hour is late and I will not decide this in a passage. Hale, you will remain with me. Child, you will have a room in the east wing and supper brought up, and we will speak at first light." He keeps the register copy, and the key chain stays clenched in his fist.

It isn't a win, but it's not a loss. Lord Edric believes the truth of the charter, he just doesn't yet believe about Hale. The kitchen staff are on your side, Tobin is by your elbow, and Brother Osric is writing his attestation tonight. Garrow is somewhere in the house, and the assessor is a day and a half off.

You step between the two men and press the copy into Lord Edric's trembling hands. Your Persuasion check was a 17.

He reads it standing, lips moving, and then reads it again. When he looks up, the fear in his face has changed into something older and steadier. "Maud Fenn," he says. "My grandmother. "Corvin will not be pleased," he says softly. Then he goes, with the gate-men a pace behind.

The study is quiet. Lord Edric sinks into his chair, the register copy in his lap. "What do we do now, child? The assessor comes the day after tomorrow, and I will not lie to her again."

Garrow hasn't been seen since the kitchen, and Corvin himself is still somewhere upriver. You've earned 50 XP.

entries.text:
Marta Pell sees the brass lantern and her whole face opens. "Bless you, child, of course. Bed, bread and a stable, no coin asked. That's the Rest's way." She takes Biscuit's rein herself.

Over a bowl of onion stew by the hearth, you ask about the wagon, and your Persuasion check of 20 gets everything. It stopped at noon. The driver watered the horses, and a sharp-faced man in a brown coat asked after "a girl with a lute" and didn't like her answer. Then a tall man in a dark cloak stepped down from the wagon's shadow to light a candle at her porch lamp. He bowed to her like a lord, paid for bread, and left within the hour for Ashby Weir.

Marta hesitates. "He left a word for you, if you came. He said you'd know him by it: *tell her the lamp is still lit for her.*" She frowns. "Is he your father, love? He spoke so gently."

The words settle in your chest like a hook. Corvin knew you'd follow, and he's waiting.

The common room is warm and the bunks are clean. A single other traveller, a snoring drover, sleeps in the corner. The wagon is half a day ahead, and Ashby Weir is another day's ride. It's a quarter past seven.

input.description: Plump, grey-haired lay-keeper of Lantern's Rest, cheerful widow in a green apron. Honest and observant.

entries.text: notebook: created an entry for Marta Pell; added 1 relationship to Marta Pell

The woman sees the brass lantern glinting in your palm and her whole face opens. Your Persuasion check was a natural 20, and your Insight, a 22, tells you she's hiding nothing. She's simply glad to see you.

"Marta Pell, keeper of the Rest, and you're welcome, daughter. Bed, bread and a stall for your mule, and no coin asked." She takes Biscuit's bridle herself. "Aye, the shrine-wagon came by about three. Watered the team, didn't stay. The driver and a sharp-faced man in a brown coat talked low by the trough, but I've good ears for a woman my age. The master will meet them at the Ashby Weir ferry-landing at dawn. And the brown-coat said..." She frowns. "'The girl has the book. The master wants her alive and the book whole.' I thought it an ugly thing to say beside a lantern."

So Corvin wants you alive, and the book intact. The dawn meeting gives you a place and a time.

Then she looks at the reliquary again and goes quiet. "Child, may I see that closer? I know that make. Sister Ansel, the old road-priest who kept this house before me, cast lamps like it. She gave them to apprentices and to the dying, and she wrote down every one in the shrine's book. If yours is one of hers, there's a name beside it." She hesitates. "I'll look tonight, if you'd like. I won't tell you what it says unless you wish to hear."

It's seven in the evening. The hearth inside is lit and there's the smell of bread. The ferry-landing is perhaps half a night's ride on, and Corvin arrives at dawn.

input.add_to_description: Day 3 evening: Marta Pell gave Wren shelter (Shelter of the Faithful) but was guarded about the wagon. Truth: the wagon stopped at dusk, the driver bought bread, and a tall, thin man in a storyteller's coat (Corvin) briefly stepped down and asked whether "a girl with a lute and a lantern-box" had come by; he left a coin for the lamp-oil and told Marta to tell no one. They went on toward Ashby Weir before dark, after the fork. Marta senses Wren is the girl, and is torn: Corvin gave her a generous coin, but the Lantern-Bearer's rule is to shelter all travelers.

entries.text:
You dismount and hold the reliquary out so the lamplight catches the brass. Your Persuasion check was a 7, which isn't enough to open her up.

The woman leans on her rake and looks at the little lantern for a long moment. "Marta Pell," she says. "Keeper here. The Lantern-Bearer's rule is a bed and bread for any who walk, so you'll have both, and your mule will have the lean-to." That much is warm and plain. But when you ask about the wagon, her eyes slide away to the road, and she says only, "Wagons come and go, child. Many stop."

Your Insight check was a 20, and it reads her clearly. She's lying by omission, and it's costing her. She is a kind woman who has been paid to be quiet and dislikes it. Her gaze keeps flicking to the lamp-pole, then to you, and to your lute, and to the reliquary. She knows who you are, or guesses.

She is waiting to see whether you'll press her, push past her, or give her a reason to choose you over the coin.

The bunkroom behind her is warm and lit, and the evening is closing in. The fork in the road sits a hundred paces off, with the Ashby road bearing north. It is nearly seven on Day 3.

"Marta Pell, love, and nobody's mother, though I'll answer to it. Come in, come in!" She takes Biscuit's rein herself and leads him to a lean-to stable with a manger of oats, clucking at him as if he were a lost child.

As she goes, she tells you what she knows. A shrine-wagon did stop at noon, just long enough to water the horses. The driver and a sharp-faced man in a brown coat were sullen and hurried, and neither stayed to eat. The brown-coated one asked whether a half-elf girl with a lute had come by, and Marta, who didn't like his tone, said no. Then they were off toward Ashby Weir. "The driver said something about meeting 'the master' at the Ashby ferry," she adds. "I thought: a master who sends his wagon ahead is a master who doesn't care to be seen on the road."

The shrine-house is plain and warm. You get a bunk in a whitewashed room, a bowl of leek-and-barley soup, and bread still hot from the oven, all free by the custom of the Lantern-Bearer's faithful. Two other pilgrims, a tinker's widow and her silent son, doze by the fire. The brass lamp burns steady in the porch.

It's seven in the evening on Day 3. The wagon is ahead of you, Corvin is said to be waiting at the Ashby ferry, and Dame Crowe reaches Thornhallow at noon tomorrow. You could sleep here and set out at first light, ask Marta more, or do something else with the evening.

The broth is thick and peppery, and Marta watches you eat with the pleasure of a woman who likes to be listened to. Your Persuasion check was a 16, and she opens up like a window.

"The lamp over the door? Master Tallowmere's gift, aye, but he never made it. It's a twin of that little brass case of yours, bigger, is all. He told me once it came from a road-priest, a woman, who died out on the Ashby road years back, with a child in her keeping." She lowers her voice. "Sister Ilwen, he called her. The child was never found, and he never said more. He asked me not to speak of it."

She takes the lamp down from its hook and sets it in your hands. It's heavy, warm from the flame, with rays pierced in the shutters. Turning it over, you find a small looped mark scratched beneath the base, and the loops are the same ones that curl through the parchment in your reliquary.

You tell her a story in return, a short, true-ish one about a lantern that walked a road by itself, and she laughs and wipes her eyes. Then she shows you a bunk in the bunkroom, with clean blankets, a candle stub and no other guests.

The evening has gone to nearly eight. Biscuit is warm in the lean-to, the road to Ashby Weir lies ahead, and Corvin's meeting is two days away. You now have a name, Sister Ilwen, and a child who was never found.

entries.text:
You sit by the hearth with the broth and ask your questions as lightly as you can. Your Persuasion check was an 8, and it doesn't quite land. Marta's warmth cools a degree. "Seven years he's been a good friend to this house," she says. "He did mention an old road-priest once, who died owing him a kindness. That's all I know, and I'd not tell tales on a man who's never done me wrong." She turns the ladle in the pot and doesn't meet your eye.

The lamp is another matter. She lets you take it down from its hook, still warm, and you turn it under the light. Your Religion check was a 12. It's the twin of your reliquary: the same ray-etched lid and the same shape of hinge. Inside the base, scratched small, is a maker's mark of two crossed keys, and when you check your own reliquary, the same mark is there, worn nearly smooth. Whoever made your case made this lamp. Corvin didn't just stumble on yours.

You promise Marta a story and give her a good one, a tale of a tinker and a stubborn lantern. She laughs in the right places and softens again. The fire burns low, and a bunk waits in the back room. The wagon is a day's ride ahead, and the ford is two days off.

input.add_to_description: Marta's tale (Day 3 night): seven years ago a dying road-priest named Brother Anselm Vane, with a looped hand, was nursed at Lantern's Rest and died there. Corvin was the one who came for his things and took the brass case, saying he'd carry it to the god's greater shrine. Marta never saw it again. The lamp over the door is an ordinary brass lamp, but its base is scratched with a tiny looped "A.V." and a line of verse matching the reliquary's blessing. Anselm's grave is behind the shrine, under a pear tree.

input.description: Road-priest of the Lantern-Bearer who died at Lantern's Rest seven years ago. Wrote in a looped hand; likely author of the blessing in Wren's reliquary. Corvin collected his brass case after his death.
relationships: author of the parchment Corvin gave Wren, per [[Corvin Tallowmere]]'s hint

time: 1 hour 30 minutes later: Day 3, 8:34 PM

Your Persuasion check was a 17, and Marta warms like a banked fire. Over the broth she talks about Corvin: the clove-and-ink smell, the way he mends a hinge without being asked, the stories he tells guests.

Then she pauses. "A looped hand, you said. That's Brother Anselm. Anselm Vane." Seven years ago a road-priest came in half-dead from fever, and she nursed him through a hard winter. He wrote constantly, small looping letters, blessings for the road. He died at Lantern's Rest in the spring. "Master Tallowmere came for his things. Said he'd carry the brass case to the god's greater shrine. I never saw it again." She looks at the reliquary on your belt, and her hand goes to her mouth. "Oh, love. That's it."

She lets you hold the lamp over the door. It looks ordinary, but on the underside of its base, scratched small, are looped letters, *A.V.*, and a line of verse that matches the blessing in your reliquary. Anselm is buried behind the shrine under the pear tree.

So Corvin took a dying man's relic, and years later let you carry it. Why? Marta can't say. You promised her a story, and she settles in to hear it. It's half past eight, the fire is warm, and the wagon is a night ahead.

Your Persuasion check was a 19. Marta sets down her spoon and her face goes soft and far away.

"Seven years back, it was. Master Tallowmere came through in a hard autumn rain, carrying that very case wrapped in oilcloth, and an old road-priest leaning on his arm, Brother Ansel Wick, thin as a rake and coughing something dreadful. I put him in the back bunk and nursed him nine days." She nods at the bunkroom door. "Wrote blessings in his sleep nearly, in that looped hand of his, long tails on every letter. The last night he gave Master Tallowmere the case and said it wasn't his to keep. It was to go to whoever Corvin raised to carry it. And Corvin wept, love. I saw it."

time: 1 hour 30 minutes later: Day 3, 8:34 PM

Your Persuasion check was a 12. Marta needs very little coaxing once there's a story promised, and she talks while you eat the broth.

Corvin gave the lamp over the door seven years ago, she says. He told her it came from "a road-priest who died owing him a kindness," and he once called the man "old Ansel." She can't say more. Corvin never spoke of the priest's face or his people, only that he'd been a good man and a poor one.

She lets you take the lamp down. On its underside, scratched into the brass in looped letters you recognise at once from the parchment, is a line: *For those who walk unlit.* Beside it is a tiny lantern, drawn in the same hand. The hand is the same, the loops are the same, and the words rhyme with the blessing in your reliquary.

So the blessing is real, Ansel wrote it, and Corvin knew him. Whether Ansel meant it for you, you can't tell. Corvin's note didn't say.

You tell Marta your story after supper, as promised, a gentle one about a lantern that kept a traveller from the river, and she dabs her eyes. Then she shows you to a bunk in the warm back room. It's half past eight, the road is dark, and Ashby Weir is a day's ride on.

What does Wren do?

sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.
